images.text: I've spent a lot of time lately thinking about how I can help make the world a bit better and I've discovered that there are many ways to do it. Maybe I should have learned about this long ago, but it's never too late to start! If you look around, you will see that there are lots of small and large contributions that we can all make, every day. If you want to help people, you can donate money to a charitable organization or volunteer your time. If you want to help the environment, you can buy products from companies that follow the zero waste initiative and use sustainable resources, or you can participate in ecotourism.

We are all responsible for the world we live in so we must all find a way to contribute. We should all make a list of civic responsibilities that we are able to keep and consciously add to our responsibilities as we are able. Every day we ought to ask ourselves, “What small thing can I do today to help the people around me?” Even helping ourselves will help the rest of the world. If you want to help yourself, you can exercise and keep healthy. You can take a course and learn something new.

The healthier and better-educated our population is, the better our world will be. Healthy people are productive and don't put a strain on financial resources of the country. Educated and trained people are also better equipped to contribute to society. If we all improve ourselves, we will improve the world. So, we'd better look around, take note of where there is need, be less individualistic and make the effort to fulfill our civic responsibilities.

Modals for Obligation, Recommendation, and Intention - Review

You use modals to talk about obligation, recommendation and intention. When you use modals, you are able to be more precise about what you think and feel. It also makes certain contexts clearer for the listener or reader.

You use the first conditional to talk about events or situations that are likely to happen. You can use it talk about events in the present or the future.
Let's take a look at how to structure a first conditional sentence.

{"rows":2,"columns":3,"cells":["{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \" If\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Condition\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Result\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"If\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \" it does not rain,\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \" I'll go to the beach.\"}"],"styles":" intro_table_border instruction_table_background"}
Notice that you are using the Simple Present in the condition clause, even though you are referring to the future. You use will + verb to talk about the possible future result.

So the structure of the first conditional is:
If + Simple Present, + will + base verb
Notice that you use a comma after the condition clause. If you start the sentence with the result clause, then you do not have to use a comma.
You can use other phrases instead of if or if not to make your language more varied and sophisticated. Two alternatives you can use to introduce the condition clause are provided that and so long as.

For example:
If you come down from the tree now, I won't call the fire department.
So long as you come down from the tree now, I won't call the fire department.
Provided that you come down from the tree now, I won't call the fire department.
Provided that is more formal than if.
